blocks.text: Non-specific neck pain is neck pain, with or without referred shoulder or upper back pain, for which no specific serious or neurological cause is found. It is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems. The word "non-specific" does not mean "not real". It means that we cannot reliably identify a single damaged tissue, and that treatment is guided by the clinical pattern rather than a structural label.

A useful classification groups patients by the main impairment: neck pain with mobility deficits, neck pain with movement coordination impairments (often after whiplash), neck pain with headache, and neck pain with radiating pain [Ref – to verify]. This chapter covers the first group mainly.

items: Neck pain, often one-sided, sometimes spreading to the upper trapezius or between the shoulder blades. Pain and stiffness with sustained postures (desk work, phone use, driving) and end-range movement. Limited range of movement, often rotation and side flexion.
No neurological signs; no red flags.

rows: Where exactly, and does it spread below the elbow?
What postures or tasks aggravate it?
How long have you had it and how often has it happened before?
Any arm tingling, weakness, clumsy hands, walking problems?
Any fever, weight loss, cancer history, recent trauma?
How is your sleep, stress and workload?

items: Posture and habitual head position (observe, but do not over-interpret).
Active range: flexion, extension, rotation, side flexion; note range and pain.
Neurological screen if any arm symptoms.
Cervical flexion-rotation test for upper cervical mobility (if headache).
Segmental mobility (central and unilateral posterior-anterior pressures).
Deep neck flexor endurance (CCFT, Vol 2 Ch 4).

blocks.text: Honest note: there is no test that confirms non-specific neck pain. Tests are used to exclude other conditions and to find treatment targets.

rows: If arm symptoms are reproduced, use the radiculopathy pathway
Prone, thumbs over the spinous or articular process, gentle oscillating pressure
Comparable pain and stiffness at a level guides mobilisation
Supine, chin tucked, head lifted about 2.5 cm; time until the chin pokes or head drops
Low endurance is a training target [Ref – to verify norms]
Bilateral hand symptoms, gait change, UMN signs
Pain with arm movement rather than neck movement

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Fever, night sweats, recent infection, IV drug use
Cancer history, unexplained weight loss, constant night pain
Neck pain with chest pain, sweating, breathlessness
Sudden severe "worst ever" headache with neck stiffness

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

steps: **Arm symptoms with neurological signs?** Radiculopathy pathway.
**Neck pain with restricted, painful movement and no neuro signs:** working diagnosis non-specific neck pain with mobility deficits.
**Start** education, mobilisation or manipulation of the thoracic and cervical spine as appropriate, and exercise.

rows: Short-term pain relief and improved range [Ref – to verify]
Neck pain with mobility deficit, thoracic stiffness, no contraindication
Supine or sitting, high-velocity small-amplitude thrust after consent
Grade III to IV oscillations, 3 sets of 30 to 60 s
Symptoms spread to the arm or head
Movement limited and painful in one direction
Sitting, glide along facet plane, patient moves actively

blocks.text: Preferred starting choice: combine manual therapy with exercise. Manual therapy alone is less effective than combined care [Ref – to verify].

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Prone or band rows, scapular retraction
Shoulder shrugs and upper trapezius strengthening
Thoracic extension over a towel roll

blocks.text: Ergonomic advice: vary posture often; screen at eye level; regular movement breaks. The best posture is the next posture.

rows: Not routine for non-radiating neck pain
More relevant to radiculopathy [Ref – to verify]

items: Visit 1: screen flags, educate (good prognosis, stay active), start range exercises, consider manual therapy.
Weeks 2 to 6: strengthen deep flexors, scapular and upper back muscles; progress load.
Weeks 6 onward: endurance, work and sport demands, self-management plan for recurrences.

blocks.text: NDI, pain 0 to 10, rotation range, CCFT stage and PSFS goal. Expect meaningful change within about 4 to 6 weeks; if not, review diagnosis and contributing factors.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 34-year-old software developer has 6 weeks of right-sided neck pain, worse after long screen work, 5/10. Rotation right is 50 degrees and painful; no arm symptoms; neurological screen normal. Right C5 to C6 unilateral PA pressure reproduces her pain. Working diagnosis: non-specific neck pain with mobility deficit. Plan: thoracic manipulation and C5 to C6 mobilisation, rotation exercises, deep neck flexor and scapular training, workstation advice.

items: **Why is non-specific not a "failed" diagnosis?** It honestly states that no single structure can be identified and focuses on treatable impairments.
**Why treat the thoracic spine for neck pain?** Thoracic manipulation can reduce neck pain in the short term and improve range.
**What would make you stop cervical mobilisation?** Spreading arm symptoms, dizziness or any neurological symptom.
**Which outcome measures would you record?** NDI, NPRS, rotation range, PSFS.
**What is the key ergonomic message?** Frequent posture variation is more important than one "perfect" posture.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Exclude radiculopathy, myelopathy and serious pathology before labelling neck pain non-specific. Choose combined manual therapy and exercise.
Prescribe a progressive neck and upper back program.
